questions.q: What is the formula for gain or loss on retirement?
options: Proceeds of sale minus original cost
Accumulated depreciation minus net book value
Cost of removal minus proceeds of sale
Proceeds of sale minus cost of removal minus net book value
questions.explain: Gain or loss equals proceeds of sale, minus cost of removal, minus the net book value of the retired portion.

questions.q: A van has a $7,000 net book value, sells for $9,500, with $300 cost of removal. What is the result?
options: A $2,200 loss
A $2,200 gain
A $9,500 gain
A $7,000 loss
questions.explain: $9,500 - $300 - $7,000 = $2,200, a positive result, which is a gain.

questions.q: What happens to the gain/loss calculation when an asset's net book value is already zero?
options: The calculation cannot be performed
The retirement is automatically treated as a loss
The asset must be reinstated before it can be retired
Net book value is simply zero in the formula, so any proceeds net of removal cost become the full gain
questions.explain: The formula still applies with net book value at zero; proceeds minus cost of removal equals the full gain since there's no remaining book value to offset.

questions.q: Why does the gain/loss calculation reflect decisions made throughout earlier chapters of the asset's life?
options: Because gain/loss is set manually at retirement with no connection to prior transactions
Because gain/loss only depends on the original purchase price
Because retirement always produces a gain regardless of prior history
Because depreciation method, cost adjustments, and reclassifications all determined the net book value at retirement, a key input to the formula
questions.explain: Net book value at the time of retirement is shaped by every depreciation decision, cost adjustment, and reclassification made over the asset's life, making it the biggest input to whether a retirement shows a gain or a loss.

questions.q: A company consistently depreciates its assets too slowly relative to their real decline in value. What pattern would this tend to produce at retirement?
options: Consistent gains on retirement
Consistent losses on retirement
No effect on gain/loss outcomes
Automatic reinstatement of all retired assets
questions.explain: Under-depreciating relative to real value decline leaves net book value too high, which tends to produce losses when the asset is actually retired for its true, lower value.
